bigPicture: The night brought mixed signals from the Gulf: Iranian officials said US forces struck sites on Qeshm Island and Iran's navy said navigation aids in the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed, yet oil fell again after President Trump said new attacks were unlikely while talks continue. A drone strike on Iraq's Khor Mor gas field knocked out most of the Kurdistan region's power, Ukraine hit Russia's Kirishi refinery and Russia sent 317 drones at Ukraine a day before talks in Abu Dhabi. In markets, Nvidia's board opened an investigation into reports that its CEO was targeted by foreign intelligence, Asian chip stocks rebounded after Taiwan curbed short selling, and China's factory prices rose at the fastest pace since 2022 while consumer inflation slowed. In Poland, the Kraków gunman died in hospital as the terrorism investigation continues; socially, at least 34 migrants drowned off Senegal, and the COP31 climate summit opened in Antalya.

glossary.def: A narrow sea passage that a large share of world trade must pass through, so disruption there affects prices globally.
glossary.example: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's key oil chokepoint.

glossary.def: The extra price (or return) market participants demand because of the danger that something bad, such as a supply cut, will happen.
glossary.example: Oil fell when Trump said new strikes on Iran were unlikely, shrinking the risk premium.

glossary.def: A situation where supply of a good exceeds demand, usually pushing its price down.
glossary.example: JPMorgan estimated a 1.4 million barrel-a-day oil surplus in October.

glossary.def: A measure of the prices producers receive for goods as they leave the factory ('factory-gate' prices).
glossary.example: China's PPI rose 5.7% year on year in October 2026.

glossary.def: Borrowing shares and selling them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price and return them, keeping the difference.
glossary.example: Taiwan cut the limit on intraday short sales to calm its market.

glossary.def: The rules and practices by which a company is directed and its managers are supervised, mainly by its board of directors.
glossary.example: Nvidia's independent directors are overseeing a review of reports about the CEO.

glossary.def: The risk that government actions, such as seizures, sanctions or sudden rule changes, reduce the value of a business or investment.
glossary.example: Japan Tobacco shares fell about 16% after Russia took control of its local units.

glossary.def: Facilities essential for society and the economy, such as power plants, gas fields, water systems and telecoms.
glossary.example: A drone strike on the Khor Mor gas field cut power to most of Iraq's Kurdistan region.

glossary.def: Replacing the direct burning of fuels with electricity, e.g. heat pumps instead of gas boilers or electric cars instead of petrol cars.
glossary.example: COP31's host wants electricity to supply 35% of global final energy by 2035.

glossary.def: Everyone of working age who is either employed or unemployed (without work, available and actively looking).
glossary.example: The US labour force was 170.7 million people in October 2026.

glossary.def: The share of the working-age population that is in the labour force.
A wage adjusted for inflation, showing how much it can actually buy.
glossary.example: Polish wages rose 5.9% nominally but 1.7% in real terms in September 2026.

glossary.def: The US monthly count of jobs on business and government payrolls, excluding farm workers, from the establishment survey.
glossary.example: US payrolls rose by 165,000 in October 2026.

glossary.def: Vaccinating the contacts of an infected person, and their contacts, to build a ring of immunity that stops an outbreak spreading.
glossary.example: The Ebola vaccine trial in DR Congo uses ring vaccination.

glossary.def: Government review of foreign takeovers or investments for national-security risks, with power to block them.
glossary.example: A Chinese review body prohibited the sale of ABB's robotics business in China to SoftBank.

stories.rankWhy: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most important oil chokepoint, so every new attack there affects fuel prices, inflation and markets worldwide.

stories.title: Explosions on Iran's Qeshm Island overnight, which Iranian officials blame on US forces; Iran's navy says navigation aids in the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed
stories.what: Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island, next to the Strait of Hormuz, late on Sunday; a Hormozgan provincial official said the sites were reportedly targeted by American forces but that no vital infrastructure was damaged. The US had not confirmed the strikes in the reports read for this edition. On Monday an Iranian Revolutionary Guards Navy official told state media that navigation aids (lights and markers that guide ships) in the southern part of the strait had been destroyed and that no unauthorised vessels passed overnight; Reuters noted the claim could not be verified and the official did not say who destroyed them. On Sunday President Trump told CNN that new attacks on Iran were 'highly unlikely' if talks progress, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the two sides were not on the verge of a breakthrough and called Iran's demands outrageous. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said mediators had stopped travelling since the US midterm elections.
stories.why: The strait is a chokepoint: a narrow passage that a large share of the world's seaborne oil and gas must pass through, so even small incidents raise the risk premium (the extra price traders pay for fear of a supply cut). Mixed signals — softer words from Trump, but new explosions and Iran tightening its grip on shipping — keep both a deal and a further escalation possible. Reuters quoted analysts saying markets are pricing an optimistic de-escalation even though no US–Iran deal exists.

stories.everyday: Lower crude prices reach Polish petrol stations with a delay of days to weeks, and also depend on the złoty–dollar exchange rate, because oil is priced in dollars.
stories.rankWhy: Oil is the most important commodity for inflation everywhere; its direction after last week's 16% fall shapes fuel prices and central-bank decisions.

stories.title: Oil slips again as Trump plays down new strikes on Iran; JPMorgan says the market is heading back towards a glut
stories.what: Brent crude, the global benchmark, was down 1.5% at $96.91 a barrel at 06:29 GMT on Monday and US WTI was down 1% at $89.85, Reuters reported; an AP snapshot a little earlier showed Brent 1.8% lower at $96.60. Brent fell 16% last week, its steepest weekly drop since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. A JPMorgan report on Friday estimated that supply exceeded demand by 1.1 million barrels per day in September and 1.4 million in October, as Middle East flows recover, output rises elsewhere and demand is weak.
stories.why: Prices fell because Trump said new attacks on Iran were unlikely while talks continue, which lowers the risk premium, Reuters reported. But tankers are still being hit near Hormuz, so analyst Sugandha Sachdeva (SS WealthStreet) told Reuters a geopolitical premium remains without a real deal, while Tim Waterer (KCM Trade) said markets are unsure whether Trump's softer tone after the midterms will last. A glut (more supply than demand) normally pushes prices down until production is cut or demand recovers.

stories.title: Nvidia's board opens an independent investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort
stories.what: On Sunday, 8 November, Nvidia's board said a committee of independent directors, helped by outside lawyers, will investigate after recent reporting that chief executive Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and that it has confidence in Huang, who supports the review. AP reported that this followed Huang's acknowledgment of an intimate relationship with a business executive whom US intelligence reportedly concluded was gathering information for Beijing, according to The New York Times. Nvidia shares listed in Frankfurt fell about 6% in early European trading on Monday, Investing.com reported.
stories.why: Nvidia designs the chips that power most AI data centres and the US restricts sales of its most advanced chips to China, so any hint that its leader was targeted by Chinese intelligence raises security questions as well as governance ones. Corporate governance (the rules for how a company is run and its managers supervised) requires boards to investigate such risks independently. A FinancialJuice market wrap said Nasdaq 100 futures fell as much as 1% at the Asian open on the news before recovering.

stories.everyday: If Chinese factories charge more, the price of Chinese-made goods in Europe — from electronics to household items — can rise later; at the same time, weak Chinese demand limits what China buys from Europe.
stories.rankWhy: China is the world's biggest manufacturer, so its factory prices feed into the cost of goods sold everywhere, while weak consumer prices show soft demand in the second-largest economy.

stories.title: China's factory-gate prices rise 5.7% a year, the fastest since mid-2022, while consumer inflation slows to 0.7%
stories.what: China's producer price index (PPI, prices that factories charge for goods as they leave the factory gate) rose 5.7% in October from a year earlier, up from 5.0% in September and above the 5.3% expected in a Reuters poll — the biggest rise since June 2022. Consumer prices (CPI) rose 0.7% year on year, down from 0.9% and just below the 0.8% expected. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy, rose 0.8%, down from 1.0%.
stories.why: Reuters reported that high energy prices caused by the Middle East war raised costs in coal mining, oil and gas, chemicals and other energy-heavy industries. Those costs are not fully passed on to shoppers because household demand is weak. Capital Economics' Nguyen Hoang Nam said the energy shock would keep inflation elevated for months but fade next year, while Pinpoint's Zhang Zhiwei said strong exports may explain why Beijing has not launched big new stimulus.

stories.everyday: Chip and AI shares are a big part of global indices, so their swings also move the funds and pension savings of European investors.
stories.rankWhy: Asia's chip-heavy markets lost heavily last week; Taiwan's emergency measures and the rebound show how authorities try to stop a market rout.

stories.title: Asian stocks rebound after last week's rout; Taiwan curbs short selling and deploys a NT$500 billion stabilisation fund
stories.what: Taiwan's Taiex closed 4.9% higher on Monday, ending a seven-session losing streak, after the Financial Supervisory Commission cut the limit on intraday short sales of borrowed shares from 30% to 3% of a stock's average daily volume and raised the margin required for short sales from 90% to 130%. The National Financial Stabilization Fund, authorised on Friday, has NT$500 billion available to buy shares. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 2.3% higher at 58,775.50 (AP; Investing.com reported +2.5%, so sources differ slightly), while South Korea's Kospi gave up an early 2% gain and closed 0.81% lower at 5,018.85 as foreign investors sold for a seventh straight session. On Friday the Taiex had fallen 4.51% and TSMC 4.69%.
stories.why: Last week AI and chip stocks were sold on worries that the Democrats' midterm wins could slow AI data-centre building, AP reported. Short selling means borrowing shares and selling them, hoping to buy them back cheaper; limiting it removes some selling pressure, and a state fund buying shares adds demand. Such measures can calm panic but cannot change companies' underlying profits.

stories.everyday: It shows why Europe, including Poland, spends heavily on protecting energy infrastructure: concentrated facilities are vulnerable to cheap drones.
stories.rankWhy: A single drone cut most of the electricity supply of Iraq's Kurdish region, home to several million people, showing how the regional war hits energy systems.

stories.title: Drone strike halts Iraq's Khor Mor gas field and cuts power to most of the Kurdistan region
stories.what: An explosive-laden drone hit the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaimaniyah province of Iraq's Kurdistan region on Sunday night, causing a fire and halting production. The Kurdistan Regional Government's electricity ministry said 2,500–2,800 megawatts of generation went off the grid because gas to power stations in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok stopped; Al Jazeera reported more than 70% of the region lost power. Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties and ordered a joint investigation; no group has claimed responsibility. The same facility was hit by a drone in November 2025.
stories.why: Khor Mor's gas fuels most of the region's power plants, so one strike on one site caused a regional blackout. Al Jazeera said it was unclear whether the attack was linked to the US–Israeli war with Iran. The ministry said it was using the Dokan and Darbandikhan hydroelectric dams and plants that can burn other fuels to keep hospitals and water stations running.

stories.everyday: Two days of national mourning ended on Monday; the attack has prompted a debate on gun permits and has raised security for the 11 November Independence Day events.
stories.rankWhy: Poland's deadliest attack in decades: the gunman's death ends any trial, but the terrorism investigation and the national debate on guns and radicalisation continue.

stories.title: Kraków attack: the gunman dies in hospital; prosecutors say the terrorism investigation will continue
stories.what: The 24-year-old man who opened fire near Kraków's Main Market Square on Saturday died in hospital at about 04:30 on Monday from wounds suffered in an exchange of fire with police, Małopolska voivode (regional governor) Krzysztof Kleczar and police said; he had undergone at least three operations. Six people were killed in Kraków — four Poles, a British man and an Austrian woman — and 15 were injured, including two police officers; his father, mother and sister were found shot dead in the family flat in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, so nine people died in total besides the attacker. Investigators secured 11 firearms; the father legally owned more than ten guns, CBS reported. Polish media reported that autopsies were scheduled for Monday and that the National Prosecutor's Office will keep investigating the preparation and chronology of the attack, which it classifies as a terrorist offence.
stories.why: A suspect's death means no trial, but prosecutors still have to establish how the attack was planned and whether anyone helped. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man held 'ultranationalistic' views and appeared fascinated by far-right ideologies (CBS/AP); the motive has not been officially stated. Reports differ slightly on his age (24 in Polish reports, 25 in one wire report).

stories.everyday: US decisions on Iran, Ukraine and interest rates affect fuel prices, the dollar and security in Europe, including Poland.
stories.rankWhy: The US president's first long interview after his party's midterm defeat signals possible cabinet changes, continued pressure on the Fed and his line on Iran and Ukraine.

stories.title: Trump on '60 Minutes': the Iran war and petrol prices hurt Republicans, 'a few changes' to his cabinet are coming, and the Fed should cut rates
stories.what: In a CBS '60 Minutes' interview with Ross Douthat broadcast on Sunday, President Donald Trump said he was not on the ballot and blamed the midterm losses partly on 'bad messaging, maybe by me', voter anger over the Iran war and petrol prices. He said the Iran war had been won and that he would make the same decision again; he also cited a 'great dislike' of Israel among voters, the Times of Israel reported. He said he expects 'a few changes' in his cabinet without naming anyone, expressed confidence in Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and said Marco Rubio would stay. He again said interest rates should be much lower and criticised the Federal Reserve's board, and said the Ukraine war would end soon.
stories.why: After a midterm defeat, presidents often reshuffle staff and adjust policies to regain voters before the next election. Repeated presidential pressure on the Fed matters to markets because central-bank independence (the central bank's freedom to set rates without political orders) is what makes its inflation promises credible.

stories.everyday: EU climate policy, which COP outcomes influence, affects Polish energy bills, coal power and the cost of emissions permits.
stories.rankWhy: Nearly 200 countries negotiate how to cut emissions and pay for adaptation; decisions shape energy policy and costs for years.

stories.title: COP31 climate summit opens in Antalya with a push to raise electricity's share of energy use, and without an official US delegation
stories.what: The UN climate conference COP31 opened on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, and runs until 20 November, with a leaders' summit on 11–12 November. Türkiye holds the presidency, led by Environment Minister Murat Kurum, while Australia's Chris Bowen is President of Negotiations. Türkiye is seeking support for a voluntary goal to raise electricity's share of global final energy use from about 21% today to 35% by 2035. The US government is not taking part in the negotiations; a group of 19 US lawmakers is attending. The UN Environment Programme projects about 2.6°C of warming this century even if current pledges are fully met.
stories.why: Electrification (using electricity instead of burning fuels directly, e.g. heat pumps and electric cars) cuts emissions when power comes from clean sources, and the energy shock from the Gulf war has made energy security part of the argument. Adaptation finance is a key fight: estimates cited by A News put developing countries' needs at about $305 billion a year by 2035, against $28–32 billion of international public adaptation finance in 2024.

stories.everyday: The talks' outcome matters for Poland's security, and Russian refinery outages can affect regional diesel prices.
stories.rankWhy: Strikes on refineries and power grids are now central to the war on both sides, a day before US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.

stories.title: Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Kirishi refinery again; Russia sends 317 drones at Ukraine overnight
stories.what: Ukrainian drones struck the Kirishi refinery (KINEF) in Russia's Leningrad region overnight into Monday; Russia's second-largest refinery by volume, it can process about 20 million tonnes of crude a year. Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko confirmed hits on the industrial zone; reports of how many drones he said were downed differ (81 per Ukrinform, 113 per the Kyiv Independent), and debris hit a flat in the town. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 317 drones at Ukraine overnight, of which 276 were shot down or jammed by 08:00, with impacts recorded at 31 locations. Talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine, with European participation, are due in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November.
stories.why: Ukraine targets refineries to cut Russia's fuel export earnings and military fuel supply; Russia targets Ukraine's power grid to cause blackouts as winter begins. Senior Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv never agreed to the energy ceasefire Trump announced on 31 October.

stories.everyday: The scale of losses shapes Russia's labour shortages, its economy and its willingness to negotiate — all relevant to security on Poland's eastern border.

stories.title: Hackers say leaked Russian statistics records show about 394,000–450,000 war-related deaths; the data cannot be independently verified
stories.what: Two hacker groups, the Belarusian Cyberpartisans and Silent Crow, say they took records from the internal demography database of Rosstat, Russia's statistics service, covering death certificates from February 2022 to August 2026. The Cyberpartisans count at least 393,881 deaths where the record explicitly names the military operation as the cause; Silent Crow, using a broader method, estimates up to 450,100. The Kyiv Independent said it could not verify the records; Rosstat acknowledged cyberattacks between 29 October and 1 November but denied any leak. The independent outlet Mediazona, with BBC Russian, had by 6 November confirmed 285,881 Russian military deaths by name from open sources, a count it says is incomplete.
stories.why: Russia does not publish military casualty figures, so researchers rely on obituaries, inheritance records and leaks. Different counting rules (strictly combat deaths vs. all war-linked deaths) produce different totals, which is why the two groups differ by about 56,000.

stories.title: Israel: Eisenkot opens coalition talks, but Liberman rules out a minority government that depends on Arab parties
stories.what: Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, formally opened coalition negotiations on Sunday evening after receiving the mandate from President Isaac Herzog, starting with Naftali Bennett and with a meeting with Avigdor Liberman of Yisrael Beytenu set for Monday. stories.title: Tusk calls reports of a ban on the Independence March 'disinformation' and appeals for calm; Warsaw tightens security for 11 November
stories.what: Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on social media on Monday that nobody intends to ban the Independence March in Warsaw on 11 November, calling the speculation disinformation, and urged participants to avoid aggression and others to avoid counter-demonstrations, Euronews Polska reported. The organisers say the march will go ahead as planned, and President Karol Nawrocki confirmed on 6 November that he will attend. stories.why: After the Kraków attack, which the interior minister linked to far-right fascination, some commentators had asked whether the march should go ahead; its organisers objected to linking the attack to political groups without evidence. stories.title: European shares open flat as a week of ECB speeches begins; markets see a strong chance of a December rate rise after inflation hit 4%
stories.what: European stocks were little changed in early Monday trading — the Stoxx 600 down 0.1%, Germany's DAX flat and France's CAC 40 down 0.3% — as investors digested the Nvidia probe, Investing.com reported. ECB President Christine Lagarde and chief economist Philip Lane are among officials speaking this week. Eurostat's flash estimate put euro-area inflation at 4.0% in October, up from 3.8% in September and a three-year high, with energy prices up 20.8% on a year earlier; markets are pricing a strong likelihood of an ECB rate rise in December, Investing.com said.
stories.why: The ECB targets 2% inflation over the medium term; when inflation runs well above target, raising the interest rate makes borrowing dearer and cools demand. The current surge is mainly energy prices from the Gulf war, a supply shock, which makes the decision harder: higher rates cannot produce more oil, but they can stop high energy costs spreading into wages and other prices.

stories.what: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Buenos Aires from Montevideo on Sunday afternoon, was welcomed by President Javier Milei and visited the Casa Rosada presidential palace with him. In a speech to officials, lawmakers and diplomats he called for safeguarding democracy and dialogue, said the economy must serve people and that growth must also benefit the disadvantaged, and warned about corruption, organised crime and trafficking, America Magazine reported. stories.title: Ebola: WHO's latest report counts 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths in DR Congo; Kenya has had no new case since 19 October
stories.what: WHO's latest Disease Outbreak News, published on Friday 6 November, reported 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths from Bundibugyo-virus Ebola in DR Congo as of 3 November, with active transmission in 51 health zones. Kenya had 9 confirmed cases and 2 deaths, with no new cases since 19 October, and Nigeria reported one imported case on 20 October, who was evacuated to Switzerland. WHO rates the risk as very high in DR Congo, high for neighbouring countries and low globally, and advises against travel or trade restrictions. Two new vaccines designed for the Bundibugyo strain — from Oxford/Serum Institute of India and from Moderna — are to join a trial in the country, the UN said on 5 November.
stories.why: There is no licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo species, which is why this outbreak has grown so large; trials use 'ring vaccination', vaccinating contacts of cases and their contacts to build a ring of immunity. The case fatality ratio (share of confirmed cases who die) is about 49%.

stories.title: US researchers link a muscle protein, Miro1, to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes
stories.what: A study in Nature Communications led by senior author John P. Kirwan found that the protein Miro1 builds up in the skeletal muscle of people with type 2 diabetes and appears to interfere with insulin signalling, ThePrint reported on Monday. Reducing Miro1 in mouse muscle improved glucose uptake, and in a 12-week aerobic exercise trial people who exercised had better insulin sensitivity and lower Miro1. Kirwan called the protein a new therapeutic target.
stories.why: Insulin resistance means cells respond weakly to insulin, so blood sugar stays high. The results come from mice, lab samples and a small trial; they show an association in humans, not proof that lowering Miro1 causes the improvement.
